metadata.title: Grupo Mexicano De Desarrollo, SA v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., 527 U.S. 308 (1999) (No. 98-231)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Grupo Mexicano De Desarrollo, SA v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc.

Opinion filed: 1999-06-17

Docket No.: 98-231

Citations:
• 144 L. Ed. 2d 319
• 119 S. Ct. 1961
• 527 U.S. 308
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 4189

Case holding summaries:
• “[A]n appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter.”
• "Generally, an appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter."
• plaintiff was seeking money damages only, not equitable relief
• “Because [petitioner’s] argument was neither raised nor considered below, we decline to consider it.”
• “Generally, an appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter.”
• holding that an appeal from a preliminary injunction was not rendered moot by an order granting a permanent injunction, where the issue appealed “[was] independent of [the plaintiffs’] claim on the merits” and 2 “ha[d] nothing to do with the validity of the permanent injunction”
• federal district courts lack the equitable power to enjoin prejudgment transfers of assets, as such an equitable remedy did not exist at the time federal courts were created under the Judiciary Act of 1789
• disclaiming federal courts’ inherent authority to enjoin transfer of defendant’s assets at request of unsecured contract creditor seeking money damages
• “[A]n appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter.” (emphasis added)
• rescission is an equitable remedy
• holding that a court may not enter an injunction freezing assets in action for damages where there is no equitable interest in frozen assets
• even after entry of permanent injunction, appeal from preliminary injunction may remain live under certain circumstances not relevant here
• powers of federal courts under the Judiciary Act's grant of jurisdiction over "all . . . suits in equity"
• pretrial restraint of debtor's assets in civil proceeding
• recognizing "the well-established general rule that a judgment establishing the debt was necessary before a court of equity would interfere with the debtor's use of his property."
• “The Judiciary Act of 1789 conferred on the federal courts jurisdiction over all suits . . . in equity.” (quotation marks omitted)
• "Congressional curtailment of equity powers must be respected."
• "[A] court of equity ha[s] unquestionable authority to apply its flexible and comprehensive jurisdiction in such manner as might be necessary to the right administration of justice between the parties."
• approving consent decree that set in train lengthy judicial oversight of divestiture of telephone monopoly
• "Flexibility rather than rigidity has distinguished [federal equity jurisdiction]."
• cataloging statutes regulating federal equity power
• "Generally, an appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter. We have dismissed appeals in such circumstances."
• “Notwithstanding the fusion of law and equity by the Rules of Civil Procedure, the substantive principles of Courts of Chancery remain unaffected.”
• "Plaintiff's with questionable claims would not meet the likelihood of success criterion."
• noting that the Court had previously authorized injunctions against the further dissipation of property where, among other things, “the creditor (the Government) asserted an equitable lien on the property”
• “[B]efore judgment . . . an unsecured creditor has no rights at law or in equity in the property of his debtor”
• stating that "[W]e would not be inclined to believe that it is merely a question of procedure whether a person's unencumbered assets can be frozen by general-creditor claimants beforetheir claims have been vindicated by judgment."
• “findings of fact shall not be set aside unless clearly erroneous”
• “due regard shall be given to the opportunity of the [bankruptcy] court to judge the credibility of the witnesses”
• "The debate concerning this formidable power over debtors should be conducted and resolved where such issues belong in our democracy: in the Congress."
• "A notice, recorded in the chain of title to real property, required or permitted in some jurisdictions to warn all persons that certain property is the subject matter of litigation, and that any interests acquired during the pendency of the suit are subject to its outcome."
• holding that an injunction freezing assets may not be entered in an action for damages where no lien or equitable interest in the assets is claimed
• noting that “preliminary relief available in a suit seeking equitable relief has nothing to do with the preliminary relief available in a creditor’s bill seeking . . . a legal debt”
• stating that Deckert was not on point because the underlying cause of action there was for equitable relief
• referring to a Mareva injunction as the "nuclear weapon of law"
• "The final injunction establishes that the defendant should not have been engaging in the conduct that was enjoined. " (emphasis in original)
• the injunctive power of Rule 65 depends upon traditional principles of equity jurisdiction, including the requirement that remedies at law be exhausted before seeking equitable remedies
• district court is without power pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65 to order injunctive relief preventing party from disposing of assets pending adjudication of contract claims for money damages
• federal district court exceeded its authority by issuing an injunction that prevented defendants from disposing of their assets pending adjudication of plaintiffs' claim for money damages
• “Plaintiffs with questionable claims would not meet the likelihood of success criterion.”
• finding that "the District Court had no authority to issue a preliminary injunction preventing petitioners from disposing of their assets pending adjudication of respondents' contract claim for money damages"
• "Generally, an appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction 'Floyd also requested a temporary restraining order below, though he does not argue this matter on appeal, and we need not address it. See Sicor, Inc. v. Sacks, 127 Nev. 896, 900, 266 P.3d 618, 620 (2011
• “Notwithstanding the fusion of law and equity by the [federal] Rules of Civil Procedure, the substantive principles of Courts of Chancery remain unaffected.” (quoting Stainback v. Mo Hock Ke Lok Po, 336 U.S. 368, 382 n.26 (1949))
• “[A]n appeal from the grant of a preliminary injunction becomes moot when the trial court enters a permanent injunction, because the former merges into the latter.” (emphasis added)
• stating “that equity is flexible; but in the federal system, at least, that flexibility is confined within the broad boundaries of traditional equitable relief.”
• noting that usually, if a plaintiff is found to be entitled to a permanent injunction, the earlier improper issuance of a preliminary injunction is harmless error
• "Because [petitioner's] argument was neither raised nor considered below, we decline to consider it."
• “Notwithstanding the fusion of law and equity by the Rules of Civil Procedure, the substantive principles of Courts of Chancery remain unaffected.” (quoting Stainback v. Mo Hock Ke Lok Po, 336 U.S. 368, 382 n.26 (1949))
